author: David Wildstein
title: Hudson Latino group wants Quijano for lieutenant governor - New Jersey Globe
text:
The Hudson County Latino Caucus is urging Gov. Mikie Sherrill to appoint Assembly Speaker Pro Tempore Annette Quijano as New Jersey’s next lieutenant governor, potentially elevating a veteran Union County lawmaker who recently introduced an unusual bill imposing hefty fines on people who have sex in government buildings.
In a letter to Sherrill dated September 30, the group said Quijano (D-Elizabeth) has the “executive capability, deep legislative experience, and unwavering commitment to public service” needed for the state’s No. 2 job.
The caucus also framed the appointment as a matter of representation, noting New Jersey’s large Hispanic population and arguing that Quijano is “uniquely qualified” to represent it in the executive branch.
Quijano, who has served in the Assembly since 2008 and is the first Latina to serve as Speaker Pro Tempore, would bring a long legislative record to the job.
That record now includes one of Trenton’s more eyebrow-raising bills of the year.
Earlier this month, Quijano became the sole sponsor of legislation that would prohibit “sexual activity” in state, county and municipal buildings and offices, legislative offices, courtrooms, school board facilities and other government-owned or leased buildings.
The measure is something of a paper tiger: it does not create a new criminal offense. Instead, violators would face a civil penalty of $1,000 to $5,000 for a first offense and up to $10,000 for subsequent violations. Public employees and elected officials could also be referred to the appropriate ethics body for disciplinary action. Existing criminal laws would continue to apply when conduct independently constitutes a crime.
The bill defines sexual activity broadly to include sexual penetration, sexual contact for sexual arousal or gratification, and lewdness. Quijano said in the bill statement that sexual conduct in taxpayer-funded facilities “undermines public confidence and workplace safety.”
But Quijano’s lengthy tenure also includes an unusual period when she essentially disappeared from public legislative proceedings without explaining why.
The New Jersey Globe reported in July 2022 that Quijano had not appeared once on the Assembly floor or in committee during the spring legislative session. She missed all seven Assembly voting sessions held from the beginning of the new legislative session through the end of June, along with meetings of the two committees on which she served.
Her absence actually stretched further back. A review of legislative video and audio records found that Quijano’s last formal Statehouse appearance was an Assembly voting session in March 2021, although she later participated in some remote committee meetings. During the lame-duck session later that year, she missed nearly every voting and committee session, including remotely, and had no recorded vote on a number of significant measures.
A separate review of legislative voting records published in 2021 found that Quijano had missed 446 votes during that legislative session, the second-highest total among Assembly members.
During portions of her 2022 absence, aides cast votes from Quijano’s Assembly desk under chamber procedures that required her to be somewhere in the Statehouse, and the Globe confirmed that she was in Trenton during the final voting session that June. But she repeatedly declined to explain publicly why she had been absent from legislative proceedings for so long.
Quijano has never publicly offered a detailed explanation for that prolonged absence.
She later returned to a regular legislative schedule and continued climbing the Assembly leadership ladder, moving from Majority Conference Leader to Speaker Pro Tempore. The position already places her deep in New Jersey’s gubernatorial line of succession.
The Hudson County Latino Caucus said Quijano’s record on economic development, criminal justice, health care and worker protections makes her prepared to assume an executive role immediately.
“The Hudson County Latino Caucus stands united in our belief that Assemblywoman Annette Quijano represents the very best of New Jersey’s leadership,” the group told Sherrill.
The letter was signed by caucus chair Carmen Mendiola and the organization’s executive board and copied to the Senate Judiciary Committee and Senate leadership — the officials who would become involved if Sherrill sends a lieutenant governor nominee to the Senate.
